To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
elevated concentration of Na+ may provoke Ca2+ outflux from sarcoplasmatic reticulum and thus enhance cardiac contraction force.
the elevated concentration of Na+ ions may enhance the Ca2+ release and the contraction of the heart by means of changing of the sodium gradient.

the elevated concentration of Na ions in the medium increases the contraction force in isolated rat hearts and that the mechanism of this inotropic effect is related to Na+/Ca2+-exchange and Na/Ca2+-exchange.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of the sodium gradient and the ion-transporting systems of the sarcolema and sarcoplasmatic reticulum in the positive inotropic effects of elevated sodium concentration in the heart.
the role of sodium in the contractile function of the heart.
the role of sodium ions in the regulation of cardiac contractile function.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the positive inotropic action of elevated sodium ion concentrations on cardiac contractility is caused by the sodium gradient change in the membrane, and the sodium ions may affect both the Na/Ca and the Na/K exchange.
the elevated concentration of Na+ ions in the extracellular fluid may provoke a positive inotropic effect in the rat isolated heart through a mechanism of Na+-induced Ca2+ release.
the sodium gradient between the extracellular and the sarcoplasmic medium is a significant factor in changing rat cardiac contraction function.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the positive inotropic action of elevated concentration of sodium ion is realized by means of the sodium-calcium ion exchange of the sarcolemmal and sarcoplasmatic reticulum membrane.

the sodium-induced positive inotropic effect in rat hearts is due to a direct effect of sodium ions on the sarcolemma Na/Ca2+ exchange, which in its turn provokes the release of Ca2+ from the sarcoplasmic membrane.
the sodium-induced positive inotropic effect is mediated by the Na+/Ca++ exchanger of the sarcolemmal membrane and the Na+/Ca+ exchanger of the sarcoplasmic membrane.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the sodium-induced calcium release from sarcoplismic reticulum may be a mechanism for the positive inotropic action of elevated sodium concentrations.
the sodium-induced calcium release from the sarcoplasmic network plays the main role in increasing the contractile force of the heart.
sodium ions may affect cardiac contractile function by means of changing calcium ions concentration in the cytoplasm.
